    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that at any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government.
    • Atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured person in crisis to get the life-changing aid they deserve.
    • It has been revealed that so far, we've helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10B in life-changing aid — and earned over 20,000+ five-star reviews.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that at any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government. The right assistance could transform their lives. But today, most never get it.

    Atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured person in crisis to get the life-changing aid they deserve. In the last six years, we've become the leading platform connecting people with disabilities to government benefits. We’re also quickly scaling an injury practice to help victims of accidents, misconduct, and violence get compensation from insurance.

    It has been revealed that so far, we've helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10B in life-changing aid — and earned over 20,000+ five-star reviews. And we're just getting started.

    We've raised more than $100 million from top VC firms like Forerunner, GV (Google Ventures), and True Ventures, with ambitions to create a category defining business assisting Americans in need.

    Each month, tens of thousands of Americans seek our help for a single legal matter – applying for Social Security Disability, filing a Workers’ Compensation claim – but many of these clients are actually eligible for additional aid without ever knowing it.

    Your job as Lead Attorney, Latest Verticals is to help us do right by these clients, helping them claim additional benefits through the social safety net. You’ll oversee the team of intake specialists who speak with clients who have secondary claims, evaluating the case facts and whether to connect them with an Atticus attorney or local attorney to provide legal advice and potentially take on their case.

    Industry observers note that this is a job that straddles the line between practicing the law and growing a business. It requires developing a strong understanding of multiple fields of law, and being able to accurately identify when we can help and when we cannot. But even more importantly, this job requires you to be an incredibly strong operator: you need to keep the big picture in mind and stay laser-focused on how we can achieve our goals, oftentimes finding outside-the-box ways to accomplish them. You will report to our General Manager of New Verticals and work closely with our CEO and Managing Attorney.

    On any given day, you’ll spend your time:.

    Speaking with severely injured clients trying to rebuild their lives after a catastrophic accident.

    Sourcing and vetting local counsel in individual markets, holding a high bar for representation quality and ending relationships that fall below it.

    Working with our data and insights team to identify existing clients who may have unrecognized claims in adjacent fields of law, and setting the standard for which ancillary cases we take on.

    Building the playbook for claim types we haven't handled before, starting by screening cases yourself and eventually creating the protocol our intake specialists will run at scale.

    This is a rare opportunity for an attorney to join a profitable and growing public-interest law firm and take on one of our biggest priorities as a organization.

    You can understand the nuances of various contingency fields of law and can apply them to a variety of cases (including Social Security Disability, Workers’ Compensation, Personal Injury, and more) – you don’t need to be an expert today, but you should be a fast learner.

    You can empathize with anyone and promptly build rapport and relationships while exercising good judgment, both with our clients and local counsel at law firms across the country.

    You have strong instincts and judgment as an operator – you can run effective and efficient processes, and you don’t let them run you.

    You have a demonstrated commitment to doing good and helping people.

    You’ve built a track record as a great people manager – you know how to motivate talent and hold a high bar for output.

    You have meaningful work experience outside of serving as a lawyer, ideally at a startup or other fast-paced, agile environment (e.g., a business operations team).

    Recent findings suggest that we are strongly committed to building a diverse team. If you're from a background that's underrepresented in tech, we'd love to meet you.

    This role offers a unique chance to join a startup that has strong traction (substantial funding, well-respected backers, tremendous growth, and many happy customers) but is still small enough that you can have a huge impact and play a role in shaping our success.

    We're a certified B Corporation tackling a critical social problem. Our mission to help people in need drives everything we do, and your work here will touch many lives.

    We offer competitive pay — including equity — and generous benefits:.

    Medical and dental insurance with 100% of employees and their families premiums covered.

    15 vacation days & ~20 paid holidays each year (including two weeks at end-of-year).

    $1,000 reimbursable stipend for education and training outside of work.

    Up to $1,200/year student loan repayment assistance.

    401(k) match and optional HSA/FSA.

    Humble, thoughtful, smart, fun colleagues.

    We anticipate the base salary band for this role will be between $140,000 and $175,000 in addition to equity and benefits. The salary at offer will be determined by a number of factors such as candidate's experience, knowledge, skills and abilities, as well as internal equity among our team.

    This job is fully remote and we’re committed to empowering everyone with flexibility. Work remotely, and travel to LA (on the organization dime) as needed to be with your colleagues – usually quarterly, plus offsites. We care a lot about building a great culture and we think some interactions need to happen in person, so we put a lot of thought into retreats, offsites, and other ways to gather.

    In a recent development, about six in 10 Americans remarked they have at least “some” confidence that news organizations will report the upcoming midterm election results accurately, according to a fresh national survey. But only 32% said they had “quite a bit” or “a great deal” of confidence that journalists would do the job.

    In the survey from Medill Local News Initiative and the Alliance for Trust in Media, 37% said they had either “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” that news outlets would accurately report the election results.

    It has been revealed that the survey was completed by a nationally representative sample of 1,057 U.S. adults either online or by telephone earlier this month. The findings echo other national surveys, including a Gallup survey that indicated trust in media to report “fully, accurately, and fairly” at 33% — an increase from an all-time low last year.

    In a recent development, the Medill/Alliance survey found about half of Americans said they had “not too much confidence” or “no confidence at all” in news outlets to investigate voter fraud claims thoroughly. U.S. President Donald Trump has cast doubt on elections on 70% of days since returning to office — starting with false claims about voter fraud on the first day of his second term.

    In another bleak result from the same poll, slightly more survey respondents mentioned journalists manipulate the news for political or commercial purposes than report it accurately. Across the survey, Democrats reported being more confident in (and trusting of) news organizations than Republicans. Nearly 80% of Republicans said journalists try to manipulate the news compared to 38% of independents and 24% of Democrats.

    More on the survey, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, here.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers.
    • Sources indicate that we're looking for a detail-oriented, driven Senior Accountant to join our Accounting team at an exciting time of growth for Supabase.
    • It has been revealed that in this role, you'll support the month-end close, perform analytics on financial results, assist with external audit and tax requests, and take on ad-hoc projects.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    Sources indicate that we're looking for a detail-oriented, driven Senior Accountant to join our Accounting team at an exciting time of growth for Supabase. As we continue to scale, we're expanding the team to add experience, spread responsibilities, and strengthen the processes that keep our financials accurate and timely. This is a hands-on role with real ownership and a lot of autonomy.

    It has been revealed that in this role, you'll support the month-end close, perform analytics on financial results, assist with external audit and tax requests, and take on ad-hoc projects. You'll collaborate across Finance and the wider organization, including FP&A, People/Payroll, and Legal, and work with our external audit, tax, and technical accounting partners, while contributing to the continuous improvement of our processes and controls. This role is open to candidates based in North America.

    This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

    Own key areas of the monthly, quarterly, and annual close within your assigned areas, preparing workpapers, journal entries, account reconciliations, flux analysis, and accruals in accordance with US GAAP.

    Perform detailed analytics over financial results to confirm completeness and accuracy, and investigate and communicate discrepancies promptly.

    Partner with FP&A, People/Payroll, Legal, and other teams to understand business processes, ensure proper accounting, and resolve reconciling differences.

    Support external audits and tax requests, serving as a point of contact and coordinating with external partners.

    Prepare ad-hoc analyses and support reporting requirements.

    Take initiative to recommend and implement process improvements that simplify, standardize, and streamline how we work.

    Participate in special projects, including process and system improvements.

    Handle day-to-day operational accounting activities with a high level of accuracy.

    Have 5+ years of progressive accounting experience, ideally a mix of public accounting (Major 4 preferred) and private industry.

    Have a CPA or equivalent (preferred).

    Have a strong technical accounting background and solid knowledge of US GAAP.

    Have ERP experience, and experience in tech or high-growth company accounting is a plus.

    Are willing to roll up your sleeves and dig into the details.

    Communicate clearly, both in writing and verbally, and are comfortable building relationships at all levels of the organization, including senior leadership and audit partners.

    Are self-motivated and proactive in identifying problems and proposing solutions.

    Are organized and able to manage multiple priorities and deadlines, and can switch gears quickly in a fast-paced, high-growth environment.

    Work well both independently and collaboratively, are comfortable in async teams, and navigate ambiguity with ease.

    Are energized by improving processes.

    It has been revealed that we know not everyone will meet every qualification on day one. If you're excited about this role and want to grow with us, we encourage you to apply.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Recent findings suggest that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the firm. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are vital to us.

    According to recent reports, once a year, the entire manufacturer gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Recent findings suggest that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Sources indicate that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    #181272. Tech Report: Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

    📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4369 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Press Forward gave $20 million to 205 local newsrooms over two years. Here’s how some of them spent it.

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4369 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • In a recent development, we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try upcoming things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    In a recent development, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try upcoming things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.

    According to recent reports, most local newsrooms in the U.S. have one thing in common: They need more money, and many dream of dollars they can use however they want.

    RELATED ARTICLEPress Forward awards $20 million to 205 small local newsroomsSophie CulpepperOctober 16, 2024In 2024, Press Forward, the nonprofit trying to mobilize a philanthropic army for local news, declared it would give at least 100 small local newsrooms — those with annual budgets under $1 million — just that type of unrestricted funding. Almost 1,000 newsrooms applied. Ultimately, Press Forward distributed $20 million to 205 outlets. Most of them received $100,000 each, split over two years.

    Recent findings suggest that I wondered what the recipients had done with the money, and which problems it had (or hadn’t) solved. Between May and October, I spoke or emailed with more than 30 grantees.

    Recent findings suggest that the grantees represented every U.S. state, came from cities, suburbs, and rural areas, and published in multiple languages. They included for-profits and nonprofits, print and digital-only publications, college newsrooms, and public radio stations. Statewide newsrooms with fully staffed teams like The Maine Monitor, scrappy news startups like 285 South, and community newspapers powered by freelancers and part-time staff like the Copper River Record in Alaska all received funding.

    According to recent reports, for many newsrooms, Press Forward was the first grant they’d ever applied for. “Many of the country’s newsrooms are small, and few get foundation grants,” said Press Forward executive director Dale Anglin. The open call was designed to change that and to distribute the money promptly. Grantees were required to complete two LION sustainability audits a year apart; Press Forward is analyzing that data now and will release its findings next month.1.

    RELATED ARTICLEA study of nonprofit newsrooms reveals some cracks in the model’s foundationSeth C. LewisOctober 6, 2026“People tell me that what Press Forward did was unusual and rare within philanthropy,” said María José Ramírez Braiz, founder and CEO of Midwest-based grantee Te Lo Cuento News.

    “They mentioned to us at the beginning of the grant period, before the shit hit the fan with the federal government, ‘If you need this money to keep the lights on, keep the lights on,'” said Copper River Record editor Allison Sayer, one of the paper’s two part-time staffers. “I feel that this was really a gift.”.

    Industry observers note that first-time grant applicants and recipients, in particular, stated Press Forward’s recognition gave them credibility and visibility with other funders. And publishers described the funding as a morale boost that validated low-paid work.

    Industry observers note that “It has been a life-changer, a lifesaver for us,” said Gretchen Sporleder Orr, who publishes the World Journal in southern Colorado with her husband. Her voice broke when she talked to me about the funding. “I don’t know if we would be in business right now if it wasn’t for the Press Forward money.”.

    In a recent development, the Real WV “would not still exist without Press Forward,” mentioned Stephen Baldwin, the site’s volunteer publisher. (He’s also the former minority leader for the West Virginia Senate and a pastor of two churches.) The outlet was one of eight grantees that received just two $25,000 grants over two years. “There’s not exactly a lot of capital floating around West Virginia for nonprofit news,” Baldwin said, “and without this outside impact, we wouldn’t be able to do this work.” But he hopes that the site can be less reliant on grants in the future.

    Sources indicate that the funding did not save every recipient. One grantee, Atlanta Civic Circle, shut down earlier this year. Atlanta Civic Circle did not receive its second $50,000 grant because it didn’t complete the first LION audit, Anglin remarked. (Atlanta Civic Circle did not respond to my request for an interview, but executive director Saba Long wrote on LinkedIn in June that “the funding environment for local nonprofit journalism is extraordinarily difficult right now.”) Other recipients have merged or transformed since applying for the grant.2.

    According to recent reports, RELATED ARTICLEFrom bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news”Sophie CulpepperOctober 13, 2026Medill’s annual State of Local News report, released this month, describes a local news ecosystem in a “state of precarity.” That state of precariousness helps explain how $100,000 over two years can be a “godsend,” a “miracle,” and not enough. As one grantee put it, “Right now, these are shanties built on a beach, waiting for a hurricane to come through.”.

    “Press Forward reached newsrooms that don’t have existing relationships with major national funders,” remarked Nina Ignaczak, the founder, publisher, and editor of Planet Detroit. “The challenge now is whether the commitment holds.”.

    The funding helped newsrooms keep the lights on, whether they used it to pay bills, pay down debt, make payroll, or as a buffer when something went wrong.

    Sources indicate that “The flexibility that Press Forward has given us has allowed us to fill — I wouldn’t say emergencies, but unexpected gaps,” said Richard Young, founder and executive director of CivicLex in Kentucky. It brought on a consulting editor to keep city hall coverage going after losing a reporter, and purchased fresh software. Without the funding, CivicLex likely would have had to dip into its reserves, he said.

    Bob Bonnar, publisher of the News Letter Journal in Wyoming, used the first payment from Press Forward to upgrade computers and cameras and give some staffers raises. “That chewed up the money very quickly,” he said, “and I probably should have held some of it back because the News Letter Journal ended up having a pretty rough year in 2025.” He had to use about half of the second $50,000 payment to repay an operating loan. The rest covered the remaining revenue shortfall and kept the organization in the black through the winter.

    Vandana Kumar, publisher of the California-based ethnic media outlet India Currents, described the funding as a “stabilizing force” that allowed the newsroom to keep operating despite a contraction in philanthropic giving and cuts to local government advertising.

    The Copper River Record built infrastructure to host digital ads and created a newly introduced website. It held listening sessions with Native villages in its coverage area and donated subscriptions to local Tribal offices. It improved the design of its print newspaper. Sayer paid freelancers to complete Press Pass training and pursued other professional development. And she was able to take on more ambitious stories about PFAS and “forever chemicals.”.

    In a recent development, the Press Forward funding was “the biggest single windfall in nearly 20 years for our small community newspaper,” Sandpoint Reader publisher Ben Olson told me. The Idaho-based paper used the money to travel to the state capital for Press Club awards and design a upcoming media kit, which Olson mentioned has improved ad sales. The Reader also paid a large chunk of its printing bill, paid its rent a year in advance, and gave staffers bonuses. (The bonuses helped the paper become 100% employee-owned; Olson’s two employees bought in when Olson’s business partner and co-owner retired.).

    According to recent reports, the open-ended nature of the grants gave Colorado’s World Journal “the flexibility to be able to make a change, do a thing, and then pivot as needed,” Sporleder Orr mentioned. “When we were in the toilet, all I could think about was, like, ‘Is there going to be anything in the post office today so that I can make payroll?’ ‘Oh, my God, we’ve got to pay rent.’” Sometimes she and her husband skipped their own paychecks to pay staff. The grant gave them “emotional bandwidth” to plan ahead.

    Many grantees used the funding to hire full- or part-time staffers. Sometimes, that worked out well.

    According to recent reports, the Mānoa Mirror, an online newsroom based at the University of Hawaii at Mānoa, received two $25,000 grants, which it used to hire a managing editor, a student editorial coordinator, three student reporters, and a social media producer. (The managing editor was paid a stipend, and the other positions were part-time.) The work had previously depended on “faculty goodwill and volunteerism, which was not sustainable for long,” noted Hye-ryeon Lee, who was professor and chair of the school of communication and information until retiring this summer. With the fresh hires, the site went from publishing a few stories a month to publishing daily.

    The Real WV’s first LION audit pointed to a need its small team had already recognized: hiring someone to sell ads. It hired a public school teacher with sales experience (including selling ads for the yearbook) part-time.

    The funding allowed Te Lo Cuento News to pay contributors consistently and to add contract, part-time positions including a sales manager, an office administrator, and a couple of reporters. The only position it could sustain beyond the grant period is the part-time sales manager, Ramírez Braiz said.

    Industry observers note that the Texas Spur is one of five weekly newspapers owned by Paragraph Ranch Media. Originally, the team planned to use the Press Forward grant to secure a loan to improve manufacturer housing and hire a journalist based in Spur (population 863 as of 2020). But nobody took the newspaper up on the free housing offer, noted editor and general manager Barbara Brannon. So the company hired four early-career journalists (two full-time, two part-time) living in its 10-county coverage area. Three of the four left for jobs in other industries halfway through their second year. The one who stayed is doing well as a regional sports reporter, Brannon said, and a hire who replaced a person who left is now managing editor for The Post Dispatch.3.

    Recent findings suggest that the turnover Brannon experienced isn’t unique to Spur. Other newsrooms also found hiring with grant money challenging.

    Sometimes, that was because of location. “Had we been able to find the right people from the outset, I believe the grant would have had a greater impact on the business,” stated Anton Kaufer, regional publisher for Hagadone Media Montana. In rural Northwest Montana, though, recruiting and retaining staff is a challenge, and Hagadone’s Mineral Independent struggled to replace its salesperson and office manager after they retired. The experience “reinforced for us that sustainability isn’t just about having the funding,” Kaufer said. “It’s also about having the people in place to make the most of it.”.

    The World Journal tried placing an ad for a salesperson with the Colorado Press Association and got “absolutely no interest,” Sporleder Orr stated. “People living in northern Colorado don’t particularly want to come live in a teeny-tiny town in a rural, broke part of the state.” (She credited the grant with giving her the mental space to fire a salesperson who wasn’t working out, then regroup.).

    Recent findings suggest that other times, the money just wasn’t enough. “The reality is that $100,000 over two years isn’t a lot,” one grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. “You can’t hire somebody with that.”.

    EcoRI’s experience illustrates those limitations. Before receiving the Press Forward grant, EcoRI had used other grant funding and reserves to hire a director of development in a one-year contract position. In its grant application to Press Forward, the team proposed converting that role into a full-time staff position with benefits.

    In a recent development, the salary limited the hiring pool, though. The development director position paid $65,000 a year, which “is really not the market rate for a director of development” in the area, publisher and cofounder Jo Detz said. (She said it should be more like $90,000.) The staffer they ended up hiring came from another state and hadn’t worked in news before. In a staff position, he cost more than he was bringing in. Detz laid him off and eliminated the position last December. She called the experience “heartbreaking.”.

    “At the point where I knew this wasn’t working,” she mentioned, “there wasn’t enough runway to pivot, rethink, rehire.”.

    It has been revealed that beyond the salary limitations, Detz thinks the development director didn’t have enough runway to succeed. The kind of development the staffer was hired to oversee — major gifts and individual giving — is a long game; “that position would need at least two or three years to begin to see some benefits,” she noted. Now, she’s back where she started, juggling fundraising with her other work.

    “I know it’s crazy to say that $100,000 over two years wasn’t enough,” she said, “but it was not enough to make a meaningful difference to our revenue strategy.”.

    Planet Detroit’s Ignaczak was in a unique position: Around the same time the newsroom received the Press Forward grant, Planet Detroit also received a $500,000 three-year grant from the MacArthur Foundation. That grant allowed her to hire a managing editor, she said.

    In a recent development, ignaczak believes general operating support is what small nonprofit newsrooms need. But to be effective, “I really think fully funding a revenue role for a minimum of three years is what needs to happen to build sustainability, if that is the goal,” she stated. “And $100,000 over two years is not enough to achieve that.”.

    In a recent development, notiVisión Georgia, a Spanish-language local news outlet with one full-time staffer, is committed to print in a world moving away from it. The print newspaper is the only way the outlet has been able to use to “generate real economic value,” said CEO Mónica Pirela, because it’s where local companies want to place ads. The organization spent some of its Press Forward funds on printing and distribution. Pirela wears “every hat” right now, and the organization’s top need is a dedicated sales manager, she said.

    Recent findings suggest that california’s BenitoLink, meanwhile, used some of the Press Forward funding to begin printing in 2025. That will allow it to apply for newspaper of record status and get paid for running legal notices.

    Industry observers note that in Minnesota, Swift County Monitor-News publisher and owner Reed Anfinson called the grant a “godsend” at a time when tariffs and rising gas prices have driven up printing and delivery costs and weakened advertisers’ budgets. The for-profit Monitor-News put some of its Press Forward funding toward redesigning its print newspaper. Anfinson also purchased materials as part of an “Out of Sight/Out of Mind” advertising campaign stressing the value of print. (He created the campaign himself, using Midjourney for the images.) For news organizations in small towns, Anfinson believes, digital revenue will never be enough to sustain operations.

    Some organizations used the funding to expand their remit beyond news.

    Recent findings suggest that for instance, the Copper River Record partnered with the Copper River Native Association to include weekly language graphics in the paper for Ahtna, a critically endangered language, coordinating with a local kindergarten class. That project required a lot of time and investment up front, Sayer remarked, but it can continue beyond the life of the grant.

    Sources indicate that planet Detroit used some Press Forward funding for reporting, but “the most significant thing the grant made possible wasn’t any single story,” Ignaczak noted. The grant gave the team time to work on its Civic Action Toolbox, which turns reporting into civic engagement prompts. In a story about a local ballot proposal, for instance, the embedded toolbox flags upcoming public meetings, links to contact information for local representatives, and suggests an organization to follow. The tool is also in beta testing with other newsrooms.

    Sources indicate that “The whole project came from having the space to ask what our readers actually need from us beyond information, and then building toward that,” Ignaczak stated. “Unrestricted funding makes that kind of work possible.”.

    It has been revealed that anfinson of the Monitor-News took the unusual step of writing a grant application on behalf of the local school district, which was losing students to adjacent districts. He used some of the Press Forward funding to match a $2,500 grant to the district. The district then ran $5,000 in ads in a “goodwill effort” to stem declining enrollment. The partnership helped to raise the Monitor-News’s profile, he stated, by highlighting the benefits of newspaper advertising.

    Press Forward required grantees to complete two LION sustainability audits. But it also offered optional coaching via the media consulting company Blue Engine to help implement the first audit’s recommendations. Of the 205 grantees, 154 participated in coaching, Anglin said.

    It has been revealed that the coaching kicked off in January, with most individual coaches and grantees meeting monthly. Multiple participants remarked the support would have been more beneficial if it were introduced earlier. This was a tradeoff of Press Forward moving rapidly to get money out the door, Anglin said.4.

    This was the first large, unrestricted grant Austin Common had ever received, and it struggled with how to spend the money. “It felt like a lot of pressure,” said Amy Stansbury, the site’s editor-in-chief and only full-time staffer.

    Stansbury wanted to bring on the organization’s first full-time employees, but didn’t want to make those hires (and spend all the grant money) until she had a clear proposal. The coaching helped her figure out which hires made the most strategic sense and how to budget for them.

    Sources indicate that A few publishers were lukewarm about the substance of the coaching, but the majority I heard from were enthusiastic. At first, Baldwin was skeptical and worried the coaching might amount to “checking a box.” In practice, though, he remarked it’s been “tremendously helpful” for tasks like writing the job description for the Real WV’s sales position.

    Sporleder Orr called the coaching “incredible.” The monthly sessions helped her with everything from tackling grant proposals to improving her Google Analytics skills. The combination of money and coaching, she added, “makes sure that the recipients don’t just continue doing business as usual.”.

    In addition to the funding, Press Forward paid for grantees to attend conferences. Anglin said 111 grantees attended the Lenfest News Philanthropy Summit in Philadelphia in 2025, 81 attended the same conference (which I also attended) in 2026, and 87 attended the Business of Local conference in Salt Lake City in 2025. A handful of grantees attended affinity conferences.

    Stansbury found attending conferences for the first time helpful and eye-opening. It taught her “there’s this secret shadow world of [invitation-only] foundation and grant funding.” Press Forward’s travel support to attend a national conference was “transformative” for India Currents, Kumar mentioned, giving it visibility and access to relationship-building.

    It has been revealed that to small newsrooms, the grant felt like a Press Forward stamp of approval that put them on the map for other funders. The Mirror’s Lee called the Press Forward funding “instrumental” in securing a $20,000 grant from a local foundation. But that was an exception among publishers I heard from; most didn’t feel the visibility and credibility conferred by the grant directly translated to other funders giving them more money.

    Recent findings suggest that so several publishers, including Ramírez Braiz of Te Lo Cuento News, would like to see Press Forward go a step further and make individual introductions to funders. “Those more personal introductions can make a major difference for small organizations,” she said.

    Ramírez Braiz also called for “more shared learning around outcomes and impact.” Few grantees had a good sense of what others in the cohort were up to, and some were interested in more knowledge sharing with peer organizations, though the day-to-day grind of keeping one’s own newsroom running was a common impediment.

    Industry observers note that since 2023, Anglin said, Press Forward’s network of more than 130 funders has invested $258 million directly in newsrooms. That suggests that over half of the more than $400 million the coalition indicates it’s invested has gone to newsrooms.

    When Press Forward first announced the direct funding for newsrooms, it “felt really awesome,” the grantee who asked to stay anonymous told me. To the grantee, it was meaningful to see Press Forward give funding to more organizations than planned in response to the scale of need. But when Press Forward went on to a second funding round in which single organizations, including both newsrooms and newsroom-adjacent organizations like the International Women’s Media Foundation and LION, received as much as $1.5 million for infrastructure projects, the same grantee said it felt like “a slap in the face.”.

    Sources indicate that “Many of the problems newsrooms face aren’t unique to them individually,” Anglin said. “If we are attempting to solve problems at scale, we have to intervene not just at the newsroom level, but at the systems level, too.” She said that because many of the infrastructure grantees serve multiple newsrooms, “investing in them creates a multiplier effect across the industry.”.

    The argument that funding support organizations and infrastructure lifts more boats is “a cop-out,” this publisher said. “I think the philanthropists know it, I think the associations know it, and I think the potential grantees that are not funders or associations or intermediaries know it.”.

    It has been revealed that young had a different perspective. Because of CivicLex’s broad scope, it seeks out funding from both democracy funders and journalism funders. Young thinks local news funders are way ahead on getting dollars into local communities.

    Sources indicate that “I think Press Forward has done one of the more effective jobs of anything I’ve seen in the broader landscape of my world, and the civic renewal space, of delivering resources to the local level,” he remarked. (He added, “No one is ever happy in the local news ecosystem when I say that folks in the local news ecosystem don’t know how good they have it. That does not win me a lot of friends.”).

    Most publishers I heard from see grants like this as critical to continued operation, yet they’re wary of overreliance on philanthropy.

    Sources indicate that young said he’d be surprised if local news is still a focus for national philanthropy in eight years. “Filling your cup up with money that will be impossible to recover in four years is a danger zone,” he added.

    It has been revealed that right now, more than 80% of Planet Detroit’s revenue mix comes from foundations. Ignaczak remarked the organization hopes to bring that down to 50% by 2028. “But for nonprofit newsrooms covering environmental and public health issues in a mid-size metro, general operating grants aren’t a crutch,” she said. “They’re infrastructure.”.

    As for Press Forward, “Time will tell, as these grants go away, what impact [they’ve] actually had on the newsrooms that received [them], how many have managed to build sustainability,” she added. “I think a newsroom that needed $50,000 to survive to next year had problems that $50,000 isn’t going to solve.”.

    LOOKOUT executive director Jake Hylton believes there’s enough funding to go around. “While there may not be enough to support every single newsroom at a very large amount,” he said, “I do believe that there is a larger investment in news that could be done.”.

    A second grantee who asked to stay anonymous was blunt about their fears for the future. “We’re scared shitless about 2027,” this person mentioned, “because not only is the Press Forward money not returning, we also see none of the national grants that sustained us in 2024 and previous years.”.

    According to recent reports, the Copper River Record was in the black before receiving this grant, and the lean paper’s fixed overhead remains low. For the Record, Press Forward has been like “a fairy godmother,” Sayer stated.

    Industry observers note that “I’m not going to lie: I will miss having the money to say yes to any reasonable story,” she continued. “But I think that, even going back to our original budget, the strength of what we learned will continue to help us deliver a higher quality paper that is more relevant to the communities we serve.”.

    In a recent development, the Sandpoint Reader, Olson said, is “surviving” right now. “We’d love to be thriving,” he added, “but we’re happy to continue to survive when many print publications aren’t.” He credited the Press Forward grant with giving the burned-out team “the chance to fall in love with our industry again.”.

    Sporleder Orr feels nervous about what’s ahead, but with the World Journal in a much more comfortable cash flow position, she and her husband are “in a way better mental state about the business.”.

    “We feel good about the future right now, that we are going to be able to keep going and make it,” she noted. “We’re back to, ‘This is what we do ’til we die.'”.

    #181265. Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

    📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 26m • 📚 Deep Dive (5107 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

    📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5107 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Industry observers note that we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • Grokipedia shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Industry observers note that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Grokipedia shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.

    Recent findings suggest that when I saw Grokipedia’s articles about me, the memories came rushing back: my 19 years in minor league baseball, including that impressive season with the Montgomery Rebels when I hit 20 home runs. I was lean back then — 6 feet tall and 168 pounds — and earned a career batting average just under .300. I became a minor league coach and managed the Chicago White Sox for a short stint in 1970, which Grokipedia stated “highlighted [my] readiness for higher-level responsibilities.”.

    I then attended Arizona State University, switched to a career in journalism, created the fact-checking site PolitiFact, won a Pulitzer Prize, and now teach journalism at Duke University.

    In a recent development, ah, the memories!…except that I never played minor league baseball, never managed the White Sox, and can only dream about being 6 feet tall. (I’m 5’8″.) Grokipedia, the AI-written encyclopedia of Elon Musk, has confused me with Marion Danne “Bill” Adair, who died in 2002.

    That article and another one about “Bill Adair (journalist)” — which really is me — illustrate the many flaws of Grokipedia, which launched a year ago. The articles are littered with mistakes and superfluous details. They are terribly written and ridiculously long. If Grok, the AI engine that wrote this turgid prose, were a student in one of my writing courses, I would give it a D. (Editor’s note: After this article was published, someone updated the inaccurate Grok pages. The original versions are linked here.).

    It has been revealed that still, the articles provide valuable lessons for Wikipedia editors who are debating how and when to use AI. Grokipedia adds new content and context that Wikipedia often lacks. It indicates that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet and summarizing them in sweeping prose. It can also provide balance to articles that need it.

    Grok can’t write worth a lick, but it shows how Wikipedia can take advantage of AI at a time when overworked editors are trying to keep the encyclopedia alive.

    Musk released Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he said was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet. With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a upcoming version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.” When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had big aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video. Maybe someday. For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia indicates edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make. Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk. Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors demonstrated Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too rapidly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a big scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s crucial and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

    Musk launched Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he said was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet.

    With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a latest version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.”.

    When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had significant aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video.

    Sources indicate that for now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia shows edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make.

    Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk.

    Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “Newly introduced pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities.     Sources indicate that right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each manufacturer’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft said they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.”.

    Anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI says it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year.

    Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an important step,” writing in a tweet that the manufacturer supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

    Google’s Next Upgrade Won’t Touch The Index, And Nobody Will Announce It via @sejournal, @DuaneForrester

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the viral version of Google’s latest research post claims the model makes itself smarter, and the post itself says something more useful to anyone whose job depends on what Google remembers about their organization.
    • Industry observers note that in March I argued that the training data cutoff had become a ranking factor, because content on the two sides of the cutoff lives in different systems with different confidence behavior, and I suggested timing important claims to land before major training runs.
    • According to recent reports, the post describes a two-phase lifecycle.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the viral version of Google’s latest research post claims the model makes itself smarter, and the post itself says something more useful to anyone whose job depends on what Google remembers about their organization. On Oct. 27, Ali Behrouz and Vahab Mirrokni of Google Research published the sleep framework, a method that gives a language model a scheduled offline phase in which it moves what it picked up during use into its long-term weights, then rehearses on data it generates for itself. The viral framing is wrong in a specific way: the post states that the method operates within a fixed architecture under human-defined training rules, so nothing is modifying itself without supervision. What that framing misses is the part that matters here. If this design ships, the knowledge inside Google’s models stops being frozen at a cutoff and starts updating on a cycle that nobody outside Google will see.

    Industry observers note that in March I argued that the training data cutoff had become a ranking factor, because content on the two sides of the cutoff lives in different systems with different confidence behavior, and I suggested timing important claims to land before major training runs. That advice assumed the cutoff was a wall with a date on it. This paper describes a wall that moves on its own schedule, without a date, and the right way to read it is as the next form of the Google upgrade: one that changes what the model believes rather than how the index is ranked, and that arrives with no announcement because there is no event to announce.

    According to recent reports, the post describes a two-phase lifecycle. During a wake phase, the model takes input and holds new information in fast, short-term memory components, which is roughly what context does today. During a sleep phase, it stops taking input and runs two stages. The first is consolidation. The model unlocks new, previously dormant low-rank experts inside a mixture-of-experts layout, assigns them to slower-updating memory blocks, and distills the short-term traces into them through a process the authors call knowledge seeding, which in plain terms means the new facts get their own fresh parameters rather than being written over old ones. Then the temporary parameters are reset so the capacity can be reused. The second stage is what the authors call dreaming. The model generates synthetic samples by randomly routing across its experts so that knowledge from different domains mixes, filters those samples with a gradient-based selection method, and fine-tunes on the ones that survive.

    Recent findings suggest that the reported results come from four settings: sequential translation into languages the model had never seen, where standard fine-tuning and in-context approaches forgot earlier languages, and the sleep model held a near-zero performance drop; recall on a long-context benchmark out to ten million tokens; factual knowledge incorporation from document passages, where the sleep model beat supervised fine-tuning and a prior self-editing method; and math reasoning on an open 8-billion-parameter base model. The underlying paper has been on arXiv since June and on OpenReview since September 2025, so the blog post is Google deciding to say this out loud, not Google discovering it.

    This is not a one-off. The same authors published Nested Learning in November 2025 with the Hope architecture and the idea of a continuum memory system, a chain of memory blocks that update at different frequencies, with the fast blocks holding short-term information and the slow blocks holding durable knowledge. The sleep framework is what you build once you have blocks that update at different rates: a schedule for moving information from the fast ones to the slow ones. Titans came before Hope, Hope came before sleep, and the arc now runs about two years. The autoregressive ranking paper I covered in September closed a five-year arc on how results get ordered. This one is younger and just as deliberate.

    It is research, not a product. The post makes no statement about deployment, timelines, or which Google models might use it. The experiments run on open Qwen models at 1.7 and 8 billion parameters, not on Gemini. No compute cost is reported for a sleep cycle, and no one outside the team has replicated the results. In the experiments, the upcoming facts arrive as documents, not as user conversations or crawled web pages, so anyone claiming the model learns from your chats is extrapolating past the paper.

    Those caveats are real and they do not change things. Google publishes research arcs and then ships pieces of them, and that pattern has held often enough that the practitioner question is not whether this exact method lands but what the design tells you about the direction. The direction is a model whose long-term memory is rewritten on a cycle.

    Anyone who has done this work for more than a few years lived through the first version of this shift. Google says it updates Search thousands of times a year and shares only the ones it considers notable, and in a 2022 interview Danny Sullivan put the previous year’s experiments and quality tests above 800,000. The named core updates are the handful that get a dashboard entry. Everything else lands continuously and silently, and the industry adapted by building a diagnostic ritual around the named few: traffic moves, you check the date against the update trackers, and attribution follows.

    Recent findings suggest that retrieval already took the same path for freshness. AI Overviews and grounded answers pull upcoming pages daily with nothing announced, so a claim that silence is new would be wrong. What the sleep framework changes is which layer goes silent. Retrieval changes what the model can look up. Consolidation changes what the model believes without looking anything up. Those are different things for a brand. A retrieved fact is cited, hedged, and replaceable the next time the page is fetched. A consolidated fact is spoken with the confidence of something the model knows, and the March piece covered why that confidence difference shapes how a brand appears in an answer.

    According to recent reports, so the shape practitioners already know, revealed core updates on the outside and unannounced tweaks between them, gets a second copy one layer down: announced model versions on the outside, unannounced consolidation accumulating between them. The ranking stack does not go away and this does not replace it. It sits on top of it, in the model that writes the answer.

    The detail in the post I keep returning to is that consolidation is selective. The authors say the model is not asked to copy every detail from its short-term traces into its parameters, and the dreaming stage scores its own samples with a gradient-based filter before anything is trained on. That is a ranking function. It decides which facts the model will carry forward as durable knowledge and which it will let expire with the temporary parameters. Being seen during wake is not being learned. Being learned is what being indexed used to mean, and the thing deciding it is a loss calculation nobody outside Google can inspect.

    Three consequences follow, and the first two are my inference from the design rather than claims the paper makes.

    First, the filter will favor facts that are consistent across sources. A gradient-based selection method keeps samples that reduce error broadly, and a fact that agrees with everything else the model has seen reduces error more reliably than one that contradicts a competitor’s page, a stale directory listing, or your own older content. Conflicting versions of your firm are no longer only a conflation risk at retrieval time, which I covered when German courts started holding the platform responsible for false answers, but a consolidation risk, because the version that gets learned is the one that fits best, not the one you prefer.

    It has been revealed that second, dreaming means the model rehearses on data you never published. The synthetic samples are generated by mixing experts across domains, so the model’s representation of a tech giant can shift through rehearsal with no fresh input from anyone. No competitor moved, no page changed, no revision ran, and the answer about you is different anyway. This is a candidate mechanism for a question I have been asked repeatedly this year, which is why an answer changed when nothing observable changed.

    According to recent reports, third, and this one sits in the paper’s design directly, there is a window. Between a fact entering the fast memory and the next consolidation, a correction is cheap because nothing durable has been written yet. After consolidation, fixing a false fact is no longer a matter of updating a page and waiting for a recrawl. It is unlearning, and removing one specific fact from a model’s weights without damaging the rest remains an open research problem. The term I would use is the consolidation window, the period in which a wrong fact can still be caught before the model commits it, and the uncomfortable property of the window is that its length and timing are unknown to you.

    Recent findings suggest that if no Google model announcement within roughly 18 months references periodic updates between releases, continual learning in production, or anything resembling a consolidation cycle, this stays a research direction, and the cutoff stays a wall. If the compute cost of a sleep cycle turns out to be comparable to a training run, the economics kill the cadence idea even if the method works. And if Google chooses to publish consolidation events the way it publishes core updates, the silence argument fails and the diagnostic ritual survives with a newly introduced row on the dashboard. I think the third is the least likely of the three, because Google has never published its unnamed changes and has said plainly that it does not intend to.

    The useful response is to stop building process around an event that may stop existing.

    The cutoff-aware calendaring I suggested in March still holds for the next major training run, because those will keep happening. What changes is the half-life of the word parametric. The safest assumption is that what the model knows about you is being revised on a schedule you cannot see, by a filter you cannot inspect, and that the only observable is the answer itself.

    In a recent development, pipelines uses Postgres logical replication and Supabase ETL, our open source replication engine written in Rust. The team works close to the database. Correctness, ordering and recovery matter there as much as speed.

    Run 1:1s, performance management, career development, and onboarding for your direct reports.

    Know Postgres replication well, including logical replication, the WAL and replication slots, and how they affect a production database.

    “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”.

    Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

    But not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

    Sources indicate that “Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres mentioned. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”.

    Mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

    To reach fresh audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres said she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    In a recent development, from the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

    “The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” stated Torres, who is right now a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    According to recent reports, another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Mongabay now plans its multimedia packages for big investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres noted. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”.

    Industry observers note that not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

    In a recent development, “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres remarked. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”.

    CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

    “We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he remarked. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”.

    Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

    Recent findings suggest that RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler remarked. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”.

    Sources indicate that looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.).

    Today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler remarked. Only 21% were “doom only.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

    “We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres noted. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”.

    In a recent development, what video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler said.).

    In a recent development, “I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler remarked. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”.

    Part of the problem, he mentioned, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”.
