    Google Publishes Guidance For Google-Agent Crawler via @sejournal, @martinibuster

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (745 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, google published upcoming guidance on how to keep from blocking its user-triggered AI agents that identify themselves as Google-Agent.
    • Google’s new guidance on Google-Agent may be related to its announcement of the expansion of Personal Intelligence, which came after this article was originally published.
    • Personal Intelligence enables Google to draw on information from across its products and services to better understand what users want to accomplish and provide increasingly personalized assistance.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, google published upcoming guidance on how to keep from blocking its user-triggered AI agents that identify themselves as Google-Agent. The new documentation highlights how to verify legitimate Google-Agent requests and configure firewalls to allow them on websites.

    Google’s new guidance on Google-Agent may be related to its announcement of the expansion of Personal Intelligence, which came after this article was originally published. Both developments are consistent with Google CEO Sundar Pichai’s description of a unified experience across Google’s products and services that’s mediated by an agentic layer.

    Personal Intelligence enables Google to draw on information from across its products and services to better understand what users want to accomplish and provide increasingly personalized assistance.

    Google’s announcement offers an example of how this works:.

    “So if you’ve been researching and planning for a trip, you can pick up right where you left off in a latest search thread without starting over or repeating yourself.”.

    Sources indicate that planning a trip can involve researching destinations, comparing accommodations, and making reservations. That’s precisely the kind of task-based search where user-triggered AI agents may fetch information from websites, interact with them, and complete tasks on behalf of users.

    What makes the timing of Google’s Google-Agent guidance interesting is that Google is simultaneously expanding its ability to understand what users want to accomplish and publishing guidance for website owners on how to make sure that user-triggered AI agents are not blocked from accessing websites.

    Although Google has not explicitly connected Google-Agent to Personal Intelligence, the two developments appear to complement each other in terms of Google’s larger goal of creating a personalized, task-based Search experience.

    According to recent reports, google-Agent is the name used by AI agents hosted on Google’s infrastructure that navigate websites and perform actions on behalf of users. Google’s guidance and also Google’s User-Triggered Fetcher documentation do not identify which Google products or services use Google-Agent. Neither documentation mentions Google Search, AI Mode, Gemini, or any other Google product.

    It describes Google-Agent as agents that are hosted on Google’s infrastructure, interact with and navigate websites, and complete tasks on behalf of a user.

    The document says or implies that the Google-Agent does the following:.

    The new guidance explains there are three ways that website owners can verify that a request comes from Google-Agent.

    1. The request’s User-Agent header contains “Google-Agent.”.

    Sources indicate that 2. The request originates from an IP address listed in Google’s published file of user-triggered agent ranges.

    3. Only where it’s present, when the request carries a cryptographic signature under Google’s experimental Web Bot Auth protocol, which can be checked against Google’s published public keys.

    Sources indicate that the first two checks are the baseline, and the signature check adds stronger verification when it’s available. A Google-Agent bot can then be allowed through whatever bot defenses are in use once it passes those checks. Google also notes that some CDNs and bot-detection services handle this verification automatically.

    Lastly, Google offers guidance on troubleshooting when the Google-Agent is unintentionally blocked.

    Google recommends ensuring that rules allowing Google-Agent requests have higher priority and are evaluated before broader blocking rules, including:.

    If bot detection, firewall (WAF), or CDN rules only covers the initial page request, the agent will be able to land on the website but it will be unable to finish whatever task it’s there to accomplish.

    Google recommends checking that CAPTCHA challenges are disabled for verified Google-Agent requests, reviewing rate limits, IP address updates, and proxy configurations.

    “Proxy headers: Confirm that load balancers and intermediate proxies preserve the original client IP, the User-Agent header, and (for signed requests) the Signature, Signature-Input, and Signature-Agent headers.”.

    Google’s latest guidance addresses three issues to check if Google-Agent is being inadvertently blocked:.

    “Shared-IP rate limits: Confirm that per-IP rate-limiting rules account for or exempt verified Google-Agent IP ranges, as concurrent requests from multiple users share the same egress pool.

    IP range updates: Confirm that IP-based rules stay synced with the latest ranges in user-triggered-agents.json.

    Proxy headers: Confirm that load balancers and intermediate proxies preserve the original client IP, the User-Agent header, and (for signed requests) the Signature, Signature-Input, and Signature-Agent headers.”.

    Google’s newly introduced Google-Agent guidance offers tips for website owners who want to allow Google-Agent interactions, stressing that they need to make sure that legitimate Google-Agent requests can pass through security defenses without compromising protections against unwanted bots.

    After gutting newsrooms, McClatchy plans to rebuild itself around AI

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    In a recent development, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    The local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old company is no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month.

    Two months after McClatchy Media laid off more than 90 journalists nationwide, executives at the storied local newspaper chain offered a blunt assessment of its future.

    The award-winning local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old manufacturer was no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month, and its survival depended on a wholesale reinvention — centered entirely around artificial intelligence.

    From the rollout of fresh lifestyle websites that feature AI-generated articles and sponsored content to legal review and finance, executives revealed how AI is now integrated into virtually every part of the manufacturer. The demonstration comes after McClatchy, one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates, carried out deep staff cuts in September at the Miami Herald, The Kansas City Star, and more than a dozen other local news outlets. An anonymous “person close to the executive decision-making” told The New York Times the layoffs were not about AI and were instead about “business performance in some areas.”.

    A companywide blueprint presented during the meeting highlights how McClatchy is systematically outsourcing the infrastructure for local news to AI agents — and rebranding around lifestyle verticals for sports fans, outdoor enthusiasts, and true-crime junkies.

    It has been revealed that dubbed “Project Catalyst,” the companywide restructure will create an “AI-native operating model” that takes “repeated tasks off of humans” and embeds AI agents “directly into the daily workflow,” Jeff Dorsey, McClatchy’s chief operating officer, said at the town hall. Dorsey described the initiative as an effort to automate “non-core as well as core functions,” “get rid of things that just don’t offer the same value” they once did, and “provide cash, frankly, to keep the business afloat.”.

    McClatchy, which operates 29 daily newspapers across 14 states, didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment.

    Central to the rebrand is the launch of four new websites: Crime Hunter, a site devoted to “real-life crime and justice”; Saltwater South, which “celebrates the places, people and experiences that make the coastal South unlike anywhere else”; Camp & Country, a “national outdoor destination”; and Student Section, billed as “the home of the college sports fan.”.

    Each of the sites is “powered by Trend Hunter,” a company McClatchy acquired in 2024 that uses AI “to glean insights into consumer trends” and sell consumer goods like $33.91 rosemary oil “to support a healthy scalp environment,” a $249 red light therapy cap to regrow hair “without the hassle of messy serums” and $34.99 “MAGIC Mushroom Coffee” for “clarity, balance and natural energy.”.

    Little discussed, however, were the company’s local news ambitions. Kristine Sherred, chair of the Washington State NewsGuild and the food and dining reporter at The News Tribune in Tacoma, Washington, said that she and other journalists were left to wonder “why we were even invited.”.

    “Our takeaway was that it wasn’t about news,” Sherred stated. “The future McClatchy appears to be building does not seem aligned with the mission of journalism.”.

    The meeting this month offered the clearest roadmap to date about McClatchy’s all-in approach to AI as one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates navigates traffic declines, shifting consumer habits, and heavy debt obligations. It also comes at a critical moment for a media industry that seeks to modernize with AI — technology simultaneously blamed for gutting web traffic and touted as a tool to cut costs.

    According to recent reports, “There is no sector that has not been disrupted this year by AI — everyone is going through extraordinary disruption,” Hunter noted. Through a laser focus on AI-powered efficiencies, he said, the firm can turn around its fortunes. “We can win — not with yesterday’s solutions, though.”.

    For McClatchy, which has undergone aggressive cost-cutting efforts since it was acquired by Newly introduced Jersey-based hedge fund Chatham Asset Management in 2020, its pivot toward AI-generated content over the last year has been met with internal pushback and, from some readers, ridicule.

    In May, journalists at The Sacramento Bee, the Miami Herald, and other McClatchy-owned papers withheld their names from articles that were produced with its “content scaling agent,” a chatbot that repackages human-written news articles at varying lengths for different audiences — complete with reporters’ names.

    Similar resistance has played out at other news outlets. Earlier this month, for example, reporters at the Akron Beacon Journal in Ohio withheld their bylines for two weeks to protest a tool that generates AI summaries of articles that, the journalists allege, undermines their work and provides readers false information.

    Many news organizations prohibit the publication of AI-generated articles. But for McClatchy, they’ve become a core part of its business strategy and, according to Hunter, a key part of its “company-wide effort to agentify the entire enterprise.” During a contentious virtual meeting in May, Hunter pleaded with skeptical journalists to get on board or find another job.

    Anyone at McClatchy can now build AI tools to support their workflows, Rajiv Pant, McClatchy’s chief product and engineering officer, said earlier this month.

    “In every one of these, humans are at the command center, they aren’t just checking the technology’s work,” Pant remarked. “They set the direction, make the calls and own the results. The technology lets each one of them do more of the work that only they can do.”.

    Trend Hunter content — including AI-generated posts — now appears regularly across McClatchy’s local publications and social media feeds, including articles with little connection to the communities those outlets have historically served. Recent examples include a post about winter “barn jackets” in the Miami Herald and a feature about collegiate football in Texas for the Kansas City Star.

    Other posts highlight obscure beauty products and questionable health trends, including how nugget ice “has become the craze worth understanding,” how saunas have “reshaped social wellness,” and “what your poop color, shape and frequency say about your gut health.”.

    Or, as one Kansas City Star reporter put it, the layoffs have created news websites where it’s “city reporters out, shitty reporters in.”.

    “They’re trying to kind of go toward these buzzy-type topics instead of local journalism that holds people to account,” said the reporter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity due to retaliation concerns.

    In a recent development, readers, an overwhelming majority of whom are skeptical of AI use in newsrooms, have also taken notice. In a post on X, one social media user wrote that “people want the news” not “AI generated slop.” Another called into question McClatchy’s decision to publish an article — across numerous local news brands — about why the actress Scarlett Johansson “changed her magnesium supplement routine after a spray left her feet feeling dry.”.

    It has been revealed that this AI slop is what McClatchy forced a bunch of its newspapers to publish in unison a few weeks ago. Who needs real human reporters when you can have this? https://t.co/Z82Vg67WtH.

    — James (@jameslineky) September 10, 2026.

    In a recent development, given the rapid spread of AI-generated content online, McClatchy executives see the brand credibility of its legacy publications as a differentiator. Over time, Hunter said, the market will reward trust — and McClatchy is well positioned to capitalize on its local news audiences.

    “It is crucial that we have credible, accurate and relevant content,” Hunter said. “We are not running from our standards, but we’re running toward a latest model to help customers make better decisions.”.

    In recent months, as much as 20% of articles published by McClatchy newspapers were AI-generated, according to data from AI-detection manufacturer Originality.ai. (AI detection tools like Originality are imprecise in distinguishing synthetic writing from human-authored content.) Rather than building upcoming audiences, McClatchy’s use of AI-generated content could erode trust among readers, said Jon Gillham, Originality’s founder and CEO.

    Such a reality is already playing out in Washington, mentioned Sherred of the Washington State NewsGuild. Sherred’s union went on strike in May to demand “ethical limits” around the firm’s use of AI. The guild said in a statement at the time it was negotiating for “freedom to write hard-hitting news stories that take time, and not be punished if we don’t churn out clickbait.”.

    According to recent reports, “We hear this from people in the community all the time: They don’t want short snippets, they don’t want rehashed work and they don’t want AI telling them the news,” Sherred noted. “The only way you get high-quality local news is by having high-quality local reporters actually out there making it.”.

    Less than a week after McClatchy laid off journalists nationwide in September, executives sent the remaining staff an emoji-laced email announcing “fresh talent”: several executives, two reporters and three editors for its “Content Innovation Lab” — the engine behind its upcoming AI-powered lifestyle verticals.

    A recent job listing for innovation lab writers notes the “tech giant’s future depends” on an embrace of AI and the innovation lab is its “next-generation approach to content” where emerging technologies are leveraged to “fuel experimentation and productivity.”.

    “From barbecue to bourbon, water sports to hiking, and golf to college sports, we are going to develop a steady stream of reader-focused, high-quality content for national and regional audiences,” according to the job listing. Producers will use AI to launch upcoming brands “tied to dedicated communities of interest around travel, food, outdoor recreation, sports and even crime.”.

    The insights into the tech giant’s future editorial direction come on the heels of its steepest staff reduction in years, with layoffs of investigative reporters, government watchdogs, and other journalists focused on local news.

    “The city of Tacoma no longer has a city reporter,” Sherred said. “What’s the purpose of a local paper if you have no one covering your local government?”.

    Sources indicate that hired to lead the Content Innovation Lab is Patrick Stiegman, a 20-year ESPN digital veteran who, during the meeting this month, turned to sports media lingo to describe the goal behind Saltwater South, Camp & Country, and its other AI-powered lifestyle brands. By “cultivating passionate fans” around obsessive lifestyle niches, he remarked, the manufacturer seeks to leverage reader data “and monetization opportunities” to guide coverage decisions.

    Perhaps nobody put McClatchy’s pivot in starker terms than Ariel Storch, recently hired to lead an AI-powered rebrand of its video strategy.

    Sources indicate that “We make entertainment — not content, entertainment,” Storch noted during the Nov. 6 meeting. “Think about a late-night show. Nobody tunes in to be informed, they tune in to laugh. The by-product is you leave knowing about a latest movie, a new book, a new product.”.

    Recent findings suggest that building upcoming audiences is critical as the company works to claw itself out of debt, said Joe Settineri, McClatchy’s chief financial officer. Stabilizing McClatchy’s core business is necessary, he said, for the Content Innovation Lab and its other AI initiatives to be successful.

    Recent findings suggest that “Today, most of that profitability is already spoken for because, like most companies, we have a sizable amount of debt,” Settineri remarked. “Like a loan on a house, we have to pay it down or you lose the house.”.

    Mark Keierleber is an independent investigative journalist who most recently reported on media, bias, and algorithms for Straight Arrow News.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    Sources indicate that kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve. Because this part of our business is growing, we're looking for a Senior Product Marketing Manager, Scaling Creators to own how Kit wins, lands, and expands these businesses through a sales-assisted motion that sits alongside our self-serve product.

    You'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team. When these creators choose Kit and grow on it, they build more valuable businesses, and that's the outcome this role exists for.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role ideal for someone who has added an upmarket sales-led motion to a product-led tech giant before and wants their work measured in win rate and deal size.

    You'll report to Christina Lhi, Head of Marketing, and work alongside two other experienced Product Marketing Managers on Kit's product marketing team. Together, you'll keep the self-serve and sales-assisted stories feeling like one Kit.

    You'll spend a lot of your time with:.

    Our sales leadership, on who we sell to, the deal toolkit, enablement, and win/loss.

    Account Executives and Solutions Consultants, on demo narratives, discovery, and technical and migration proof.

    Product, on packaging, debuts, and roadmap input.

    RevOps and analytics, on how accounts get routed to sales, attribution, and pricing decisions.

    Creator Success, on case studies, customer references, and expansion plays.

    Demand gen, content, and events, on campaigns and events for established creators.

    Sources indicate that first Week: Dive into our onboarding curriculum in Notion and learn Kit's product, pricing, and current positioning. Attend Get-To-Know-You (GTKY) meetings with marketing, sales, Solutions Consultants, RevOps, and Creator Success. Get access to our CRM, call recordings, and product analytics, and start listening to recent sales calls. Understand how product marketing currently works at Kit.

    Industry observers note that first Month: Shadow 15+ sales calls and talk with 10 established creators, including recent wins, losses, and churned accounts. Audit the sales content reps use today and how product usage currently routes accounts to sales. Set baselines with RevOps for win rate, sales cycle, deal size, and expansion revenue. Share a written point of view with the entire growth team on who our established creator buyer is and the three biggest gaps in how we sell to them. And an action initiative on how we can win these creators.

    Recent findings suggest that first Year: Sales runs on messaging and tools you built, pitch with confidence and we drive 2X inbound MQLs from when you started. You’ll own and lead our channel strategy, setting the vision, driving cross-functional alignment, and partnering with Marketing to bring it to life. You'll run a quarterly win/loss program and share what you learn openly, build a clear path for sales leads on our website, and make sure launches that matter to larger accounts ship with both a self-serve and a sales-assisted version. Your work has a direct impact on helping Kit reach $100,000,000 ARR while protecting the self-serve engine that got us here.

    Segmentation and buyer definition: turning firmographic and product usage data into a clear picture of who to sell to and when.

    Messaging and positioning for a sales-assisted buyer, including competitive differentiation and objection handling.

    Sales enablement that reps actually use: demo narratives, discovery guides, business cases, and battlecards.

    Writing and storytelling that turns product depth into a business case a non-technical buyer can act on.

    Working with CRM, product analytics, and pipeline data to measure funnel conversion, win rate, and deal size.

    Customer and market/competitor research, including win/loss interviews and call analysis.

    Systems thinking: connecting people, processes, data, and tools to identify opportunities and build repeatable solutions across the go-to-market motion.

    Strong AI fluency: knowing when to leverage AI and how to build AI-powered workflows or tools that scale product marketing work, with human judgment and quality checks built in.

    Pricing and packaging input for a new tier or add-on (nice to have).

    7+ years in B2B SaaS product marketing, including at least 2 years supporting a sales team selling to mid-market and/or larger accounts.

    Added a sales-led motion on top of a product-led one at a high-growth organization, and can show what changed before and after with clear metrics.

    Built a deal toolkit and enablement program from little or nothing, and tied it to a sales metric like win rate or deal size.

    Ran a win/loss or customer research program that changed how a team sold or built.

    Ran an expansion or account-based program for an existing customer base (nice to have).

    Worked in email, martech, or the creator economy.

    Sources indicate that you lead without a formal title. You align sales, product, RevOps, and finance on goals, trade-offs, and what success looks like, then keep things moving.

    You advocate for creators in decisions, and you protect the self-serve experience instead of pushing every account toward sales.

    You act with urgency and stay focused on hitting OKRs and owning outcomes.

    Recent findings suggest that you work in public. You share findings, drafts, and the reasoning behind decisions so others can build on them.

    You connect data to decisions, and you help others get sharper about using it.

    You raise the bar on quality and iterate toward it, and you shape how your team uses AI, from call analysis to keeping battlecards current.

    It has been revealed that experience in only self-serve or only enterprise sales. This role lives in the space between them, and you'll need to understand both.

    Treating enablement as a deck handoff. The work includes coaching reps, measuring what gets used, and revising what doesn't land.

    Recent findings suggest that wanting a sales playbook already in place. Much of this motion doesn't exist yet, and you'll be building it as you learn.

    Preferring to be measured on output rather than outcomes. You'll share accountability with Sales for win rate, deal size, and expansion revenue.

    Needing extensive approval before acting. You'll be trusted to make calls on speed versus quality and to explain your reasoning.

    Discomfort with direct, candid feedback, especially from sellers on what's working in live deals.

    We're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time—so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    Kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we’re hiring at our level 4 ($166,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    We cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance plans through Aetna.

    In a recent development, $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Organization-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, your Black Friday advertising should now be built, paced, and approved. The useful work left is checking what’s running will continue running and being honest about anything that isn’t ready. Some of it can still be fixed in the few days before Black Friday on Nov. 27, and some of it belongs on next year’s proposal.

    It has been revealed that this is the checklist our team works through on the accounts we run through the end of the holiday season. Most of this is dull stuff, sure, but the last thing you want is something like this breaking at the worst possible time. So think of it like our checklist being passed on to you to make sure that doesn’t happen.

    In a recent development, if you have not built campaigns by now, you are really cutting it close and leaving it for last minute. For the accounts we run, the freeze date was last Friday, Nov. 20, and since then the only changes going in are fixes or tweaks. Any major changes now could trigger you right back into learning mode, and you don’t want that. Campaigns should be structured, stable, and running leading into Black Friday Cyber Monday (BFCM).

    If something still isn’t built, only launch low-risk pieces, like a brand campaign if you somehow don’t have one, or promo creative inside an asset group or ad set that already has history. Anything structural goes on next year’s initiative.

    Pacing should have started in early November, so budgets are already close to where you want them on Black Friday instead of sitting at an October level waiting for one big jump on Thursday. Frankly speaking, most companies start their BFCM offers early, so if that’s you, you have nothing to worry about here because you might already be ramped up.

    Recent findings suggest that on Meta, the ramp should have happened in steps, since frequent budget changes can send ad sets back into learning. Meta’s developer documentation describes budget scheduling as a way to “schedule budget increases for your campaign or ad set budget” for days when you expect higher sales. If you scheduled increases, check the dates and amounts against your sale.

    On Google, a campaign can spend up to twice its average daily budget on a given day, and no more than 30.4 times the average daily budget over the month. When you change a budget partway through the month, Google recalculates the monthly limit as what you’ve spent so far plus the new daily budget times the remaining calendar days, counting the day of the edit.

    Industry observers note that cyber Monday 2026 falls on Nov. 30, the last day of the month, so if you raise a budget that morning, the monthly limit becomes what you’ve spent plus one day of the new budget, and you won’t be charged for more than that one day regardless of the 2x daily allowance. A campaign that runs close to double its budget Friday through Sunday is also using the monthly room Cyber Monday would have had. So treat Black Friday through Cyber Monday as one stretch, set those budgets before the weekend, and check on Sunday night how much monthly room your key campaigns have left.

    Industry observers note that google’s campaign total budgets let you set one budget for a three- to 90-day window on Performance Max, Search, and Shopping, but they’re only available for fresh campaigns, so this isn’t the week to start using them. The monthly limit starts over on Dec. 1, so set December budgets now as well.

    It has been revealed that if budgets haven’t ramped, raise Google budgets today, since the change takes effect immediately and the rest of the month paces to the new number. On Meta, start stepping budgets up today rather than all at once on Thursday night. And write down the budget you wish you’d had on November 1, because that’s where next year’s ramp starts.

    See also: Google Ads Channel Priorities Have Limits – What PMax Still Won’t Let You Split.

    A few things can’t be checked in a settings screen, so these are the questions I’d want an honest answer to before Thursday, and what I’d do if the answer is no.

    Prospecting funded in September and October is what pays during BFCM. In our accounts, upper-funnel spend takes roughly six to eight weeks to show up in revenue, which is why I argued that September was the last month to fund it. Your own lag depends on price point and how long people take to decide.

    In a recent development, if the answer is no: Don’t launch cold prospecting this week, when in our accounts prospecting CPMs are at their highest of the year. Keep the prospecting you have on a flat budget through the week and let harvest campaigns take the extra money. Put the build on next year’s calendar for September, as a fixed budget rather than a percentage of whatever is left.

    According to recent reports, it should lean towards Bottom Of Funnel (BoFu). BFCM is when the demand you built in the fall turns into orders, so retargeting, brand search, and your existing customers are going to take a bigger share of spend than they do the rest of the year. During the holidays, those sales are worth buying. What matters is that it was a decision. Before the week starts, you should know roughly how much budget is going to people who already know you, how much stays on new customers, and what the floor is for prospecting so it doesn’t get raided the first time retargeting looks great on Friday morning.

    According to recent reports, keep in mind that during BFCM, your email, SMS, retargeting, and brand campaigns are often all reaching the same person for the same order, and each one will report it. So don’t move budget into retargeting just because its ROAS looks great on Black Friday. Check it against what the store is actually doing overall before you add more.

    It has been revealed that you can see the split on both platforms. On Google, lifecycle goal reporting adds a “New vs. returning customers” segment to the Campaigns table on campaigns where the new customer acquisition goal is turned on, and on Meta, audience segments break sales campaign results into new, engaged, and existing customers once you’ve defined them in your ad account settings.

    Industry observers note that if the answer is no: Decide it today. Write down the prospecting floor and the rough share for upcoming versus existing customers through Cyber Monday, and look at the new versus returning numbers each morning so you’re adjusting against the plan instead of against whichever campaign has the best ROAS that day.

    Recent findings suggest that you should by now. Testing is what October is for, and BFCM is when you have winning creative you know you can put advertising dollars against. That matters most on Meta, where the creative is doing most of the targeting in Advantage+, so in our accounts, a proven concept with the offer added to it tends to beat a brand fresh idea during holiday shopping. The offer can go on as an overlay, in the first few seconds of a video, or in the headline, without changing what made the ad work in the first place.

    If the answer is no: Look back at the last 60 to 90 days, pick the best performer on each platform by cost per purchase, and add the offer to that. Don’t run a creative test during the most expensive week of the year, because whatever wins under BFCM pricing won’t tell you much about January. Put an October testing window on next year’s proposal, so you go into the holiday season with your winners already picked.

    Every date through December should have creative approved and paused: Black Friday, Cyber Monday, any Cyber Week extension, shipping deadlines, last-minute gifts and gift cards, and post-Christmas on Dec. 26.

    Google’s ad review page says most ads are reviewed within one business day and “changes to your ad or assets restart the review process and may cause delays.” Meta’s Marketing API best practices say changes to creative or targeting trigger review and that an ad entering review while paused stays paused after approval.

    If the answer is no: Submit what’s missing today with final copy and schedule it with end dates, because Thanksgiving week is short on business days and a typo caught after approval means another trip through review.

    It has been revealed that place a real order with your promo code and follow it into Google Ads and Meta Events Manager. A tag check only confirms that something fired, and a checkout change made in November can alter the value your purchase event sends without stopping it from firing.

    Recent findings suggest that if something is off, it’s worth pulling a developer in before Wednesday. If tracking breaks during the week anyway, fix it and apply a data exclusion so the bidder doesn’t learn from the broken days. Cancel the test order afterward.

    It has been revealed that the site banner, landing page, sale price in your feed, Merchant Center promotions, and ad copy should all say the same thing, because a mismatch usually reveals up as disapprovals the morning the sale starts. Merchant Center’s automatic item updates are on by default and correct prices from your landing pages, but Google says they may not work for products whose price changes more than once a day.

    Push your own feed updates for any hourly doorbusters, run a purchase on the promo landing page from a phone the way a customer would, and name the person who opens Merchant Center diagnostics first thing Black Friday.

    Billing is the item most likely to stop every ad you have. Google claims a declined payment can stop the account, and on monthly invoicing, once costs reach the account budget, “all ads in the account stop running.” On Meta, the ad account spend cap is a hard stop, and “when the amount is reached, all delivery stops.”.

    Sources indicate that raise the invoiced account budget to cover the higher spend through Nov. 30, reset any Meta spend cap, check the card on file, and give at least two people admin access on both platforms and Merchant Center, with two-step verification on devices they’ll have over the holiday.

    Several Google Ads features that add promotions or pick landing pages are on by default, so go through them before your own promotion goes live.

    I wouldn’t switch all of this off on principle. Decide on each one during the holidays and note what you changed so you can revisit it in January.

    Your brand campaign should be fully funded through Cyber Monday, and even into December. Keep an eye on auction insights daily to see which competitors are bidding on your brand. I know I’m stating the obvious, but this is definitely not the time of the year to let a competitor steal a brand sale. Be defensive, buy your brand terms, and keep that impression share % high. Keeping brand in its own campaign, which I’ve argued for before, makes a “Limited By Budget” status obvious the morning it happens.

    On one premium brand we work with, several competitors were bidding on the brand name, and we’ve consistently managed brand spend throughout the year, but during holiday shopping times, we max out impression share %.

    It has been revealed that once the checks are done, the hardest part of Black Friday advertising is leaving the account alone and letting it run. Of course, make sure there is someone keeping an eye on it from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday and have a plan in place for what can change. Does pacing increase at all? If so, what % increase is the cap? Should any creative be swapped out? Messaging?

    We keep that checklist pretty short: budgets on campaigns that are hitting target and fixes for tracking or disapprovals, and everything else waits until Dec. 1.

    Industry observers note that keep a running list throughout the week of anything you couldn’t fix, whether that’s prospecting you never built, creative you didn’t get to test, or the budget you wish you’d started with in early November. It’s the most useful thing you’ll have when you start planning next year’s holiday season, and it’s a lot easier to write down this week than to piece together in January, or even next year.

    Featured Image: Master1305/Shutterstock.

    Check that budgets have ramped, that tracking records the right value on a real promo order, that billing won’t stop your ads, and that your offer matches across site, feed, and ads. Campaigns and creative should already be built, so the week is for checks and fixes.

    It has been revealed that enough that your best campaigns aren’t capped on Black Friday or Cyber Monday, based on your own past results rather than a round number. With Cyber Monday on November 30, set Google budgets before the weekend, since a budget raised on the last day of the month only gets one day of room.

    For this year, mostly yes. In our accounts, upper-funnel spend takes roughly six to eight weeks to show up in revenue, so prospecting launched now is bought at peak prices and mostly pays out in January. Keep what you have running and plan next year’s build for September.

    No. Results from BFCM week don’t carry over well to the rest of the year, and an untested concept is an expensive bet at peak prices. Put the offer on proven creative and test in October.

    Yes. If competitors bid on your brand and you don’t, you can lose those sales to them. Keep brand in its own campaign with enough budget and check auction insights daily through Cyber Week.

    Congressional Democrats will have to determine whether they want to revive the old system Donald Trump defunded or build something more attuned to today’s media ecosystem.

    According to recent reports, it was 318 days ago that the Corporation for Public Broadcasting — the primary funder of public media in the United States since 1967 — officially ceased to be, the victim of Republican budget cuts and years of attacks from Donald Trump. CPB is not “on pause” or “in hibernation” — it’s dead. As its final CEO Patricia Harrison put it: “CPB’s final act would be to protect the integrity of the public media system and democratic values by dissolving, rather than allowing the organization to remain defunded and vulnerable to additional attacks.”.

    You may have heard, however, that we had some elections in the U.S. recently, and the Republicans who defunded NPR and PBS will no longer control the House of Representatives or Senate as of January 3. In their place will be Congressional Democrats much more favorable to public media. So it seems quite likely that the federal government’s next budget will re-fund it rather than de-fund it.

    According to recent reports, but with CPB officially no more, Democrats will have a rare opportunity to rethink the system from scratch instead of just prescribing minor tweaks to funding levels. The media environment of 2027 will, it goes without saying, be radically different from 1967’s. Over-the-air broadcasting is no longer America’s dominant medium. The immensely profitable newspapers that were the bedrock of news back then are shells of their former selves. And what was once a highly localized information ecosystem has been thoroughly nationalized and globalized, with access to news increasingly determined by a few large tech platforms. Democrats could just revive the old LBJ-era model — but should they instead build something upcoming?

    Industry observers note that these questions will dominate the next year of discourse around public media, and interested parties are already laying out plans. This morning, the Roosevelt Institute released a fresh white paper titled “Creating a New U.S. Public Media System: Normative Arguments and Policy Options.” Written by Penn professor (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Victor Pickard, it argues for a thorough reinvention:.

    It has been revealed that taken together, the 2025 federal defunding of American public media, the ongoing collapse of local journalism, growing media oligarchy, a multitude of social harms arising from unregulated platforms and AI technologies, and other political and economic challenges to our media and democracy demonstrate the need for robust public media systems. Fundamental flaws — especially its funding mechanisms — are baked into the historical U.S. public media model, and they must be structurally addressed. The current crisis presents a unique opportunity to create an entirely newly introduced kind of public media system based on a local “Public Media Center” model. Pickard lays out three core ideas: de-privatization, democratization, and localization. De-privatization means more thoroughly removing “public” media from the interests of the private sector. No more sponsorship messages from Monsanto or ExxonMobil, no more need to pitch corporations or beg listeners for the funds needed to pay reporters. Pickard wants the public media system to be entirely publicly funded, to the tune of roughly $30 billion a year. That would be a massive increase — almost 60×! — from the pre-Trump level of federal funding, which was around $500 million a year. Even if you include all non-federal sources of revenue, $30 billion would still represent a public media system 8 to 10 times larger than what exists today. (Pickard dreams substantial!) RELATED ARTICLEDo countries with better-funded public media also have healthier democracies? Of course they doJoshua BentonJanuary 24, 2022But the fact that $30 billion sounds enormous is mostly about how small U.S. public media has always been compared to its international peers. Before defunding, the U.S. spent roughly $3 per person per year on public media. Compare that to countries like Norway ($110), Finland ($101), Denmark ($93), the U.K. ($81), France ($76), Czechia ($60), Japan ($53), Australia ($36), and Canada ($27). If Pickard got his $30 billion wish, U.S. public media funding would sit at about $88 per capita — BBC territory, roughly speaking. But even getting to the level of Canada or Australia would represent a huge increase. By democratization, Pickard means confronting criticism that public media systems’ output often skews toward the interests of elites — either the incumbent government in a case like Viktor Orbán’s Hungary or the sort of “latte-sipping NPR liberals” that conservatives have inveighed against for decades: Endeavoring to democratize public media institutions, therefore, is not only ethically sound but also strategic: Democratization can help ensure bipartisan trust, structural resilience, and journalistic independence. Toward this aim, a public media system should not be public in name only but actually owned and controlled by local communities. To encourage trust and community investment, this collective ownership and governance must translate to public participation in all stages of media production and dissemination. In fact, public media institutions are often cross-ideological islands of trust in an otherwise dismal landscape. This trust in public media can be further deepened through direct public ownership and participation, perhaps through community action programs, participatory budgeting, or some similar bottom-up model of democratic governance. Local media bureaus — rotating oversight boards that are locally elected or randomly selected — could help ensure additional public accountability.

    By democratization, Pickard means confronting criticism that public media systems’ output often skews toward the interests of elites — either the incumbent government in a case like Viktor Orbán’s Hungary or the sort of “latte-sipping NPR liberals” that conservatives have inveighed against for decades:.

    Endeavoring to democratize public media institutions, therefore, is not only ethically sound but also strategic: Democratization can help ensure bipartisan trust, structural resilience, and journalistic independence.     In a recent development, this trust in public media can be further deepened through direct public ownership and participation, perhaps through community action programs, participatory budgeting, or some similar bottom-up model of democratic governance. Local media bureaus — rotating oversight boards that are locally elected or randomly selected — could help ensure additional public accountability.

    Industry observers note that and for Pickard, localization is a logical response to the de-localization of media that the internet hath wrought. Many public radio and TV stations primarily serve as distributors of national content, in large part because funding is nowhere near robust enough to create enough local programming to fill each day. And no matter how much you like Ken Burns or All Things Considered, sending the same programming nationwide can limit the range of a community’s residents who might be interested. He advocates pushing more control away from a federal-level entity like CPB and toward states, counties, and cities via block grants.

    Pickard describes the nodes of this system as Public Media Centers: “multimedia hubs that are federally guaranteed but locally owned and democratically governed,” which “would provide journalism, broadcasting, digital media, and other information services based on community needs.”11“Public Media Centers” is also what Pickard called them in one of his first public articulations of the idea, in his 2021 prediction here at Nieman Lab. Some might be housed in existing public radio or TV stations, others in post offices or libraries. And individual communities would be able to determine which media formats work best for them, rather than being locked into the expensive broadcast infrastructure required to reach audiences in 1967.

    It has been revealed that I am obliged to note that there are a huge number of barriers to Pickard’s vision becoming reality. Most obviously: $30 billion a year is a lot of money. That’s around the annual budget of the federal school lunch program ($32 billion), FEMA ($32 billion), or NASA ($25 billion). Secondly, the commercial media industry would not sit quietly while the federal government funds an enormous new rival that doesn’t need to sell ads or subscriptions. (For context, the entire U.S. newspaper industry pulls in around $20 billion a year in revenue.) And American suspicion of “state-funded media” goes deep enough that I can’t imagine Democrats looking to retake the White House in 2028 deciding this is the hill to die on.

    Sources indicate that but the upcoming Congress is still weeks away from convening, and the next federal fiscal year starts more than 10 months from now. This is the season for big dreams, for expanding the edges of the Overton window, and in that sense, Pickard’s ideas should give newly empowered policymakers a lot to think about.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    Kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve. Because this part of our business is growing, we're looking for a Senior Product Marketing Manager, Scaling Creators to own how Kit wins, lands, and expands these businesses through a sales-assisted motion that sits alongside our self-serve product.

    It has been revealed that you'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team. When these creators choose Kit and grow on it, they build more valuable businesses, and that's the outcome this role exists for.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role ideal for someone who has added an upmarket sales-led motion to a product-led company before and wants their work measured in win rate and deal size.

    According to recent reports, you'll report to Christina Lhi, Head of Marketing, and work alongside two other experienced Product Marketing Managers on Kit's product marketing team. Together, you'll keep the self-serve and sales-assisted stories feeling like one Kit.

    You'll spend a lot of your time with:.

    Our sales leadership, on who we sell to, the deal toolkit, enablement, and win/loss.

    Account Executives and Solutions Consultants, on demo narratives, discovery, and technical and migration proof.

    Product, on packaging, rolls out, and roadmap input.

    RevOps and analytics, on how accounts get routed to sales, attribution, and pricing decisions.

    Creator Success, on case studies, customer references, and expansion plays.

    Demand gen, content, and events, on campaigns and events for established creators.

    First Week: Dive into our onboarding curriculum in Notion and learn Kit's product, pricing, and current positioning. Attend Get-To-Know-You (GTKY) meetings with marketing, sales, Solutions Consultants, RevOps, and Creator Success. Get access to our CRM, call recordings, and product analytics, and start listening to recent sales calls. Understand how product marketing right now works at Kit.

    Recent findings suggest that first Month: Shadow 15+ sales calls and talk with 10 established creators, including recent wins, losses, and churned accounts. Audit the sales content reps use today and how product usage right now routes accounts to sales. Set baselines with RevOps for win rate, sales cycle, deal size, and expansion revenue. Share a written point of view with the entire growth team on who our established creator buyer is and the three biggest gaps in how we sell to them. And an action plan on how we can win these creators.

    First Year: Sales runs on messaging and tools you built, pitch with confidence and we drive 2X inbound MQLs from when you started. You’ll own and lead our channel strategy, setting the vision, driving cross-functional alignment, and partnering with Marketing to bring it to life. You'll run a quarterly win/loss program and share what you learn openly, build a clear path for sales leads on our website, and make sure launches that matter to larger accounts ship with both a self-serve and a sales-assisted version. Your work has a direct impact on helping Kit reach $100,000,000 ARR while protecting the self-serve engine that got us here.

    Segmentation and buyer definition: turning firmographic and product usage data into a clear picture of who to sell to and when.

    Messaging and positioning for a sales-assisted buyer, including competitive differentiation and objection handling.

    Sales enablement that reps actually use: demo narratives, discovery guides, business cases, and battlecards.

    Writing and storytelling that turns product depth into a business case a non-technical buyer can act on.

    Working with CRM, product analytics, and pipeline data to measure funnel conversion, win rate, and deal size.

    Customer and market/competitor research, including win/loss interviews and call analysis.

    Systems thinking: connecting people, processes, data, and tools to identify opportunities and build repeatable solutions across the go-to-market motion.

    Strong AI fluency: knowing when to leverage AI and how to build AI-powered workflows or tools that scale product marketing work, with human judgment and quality checks built in.

    Pricing and packaging input for a latest tier or add-on (nice to have).

    7+ years in B2B SaaS product marketing, including at least 2 years supporting a sales team selling to mid-market and/or larger accounts.

    Added a sales-led motion on top of a product-led one at a high-growth manufacturer, and can show what changed before and after with clear metrics.

    Built a deal toolkit and enablement program from little or nothing, and tied it to a sales metric like win rate or deal size.

    Ran a win/loss or customer research program that changed how a team sold or built.

    Ran an expansion or account-based program for an existing customer base (nice to have).

    Worked in email, martech, or the creator economy.

    It has been revealed that you lead without a formal title. You align sales, product, RevOps, and finance on goals, trade-offs, and what success looks like, then keep things moving.

    You advocate for creators in decisions, and you protect the self-serve experience instead of pushing every account toward sales.

    You act with urgency and stay focused on hitting OKRs and owning outcomes.

    Industry observers note that you work in public. You share findings, drafts, and the reasoning behind decisions so others can build on them.

    You connect data to decisions, and you help others get sharper about using it.

    You raise the bar on quality and iterate toward it, and you shape how your team uses AI, from call analysis to keeping battlecards current.

    Experience in only self-serve or only enterprise sales. This role lives in the space between them, and you'll need to understand both.

    Treating enablement as a deck handoff. The work includes coaching reps, measuring what gets used, and revising what doesn't land.

    Wanting a sales playbook already in place. Much of this motion doesn't exist yet, and you'll be building it as you learn.

    Preferring to be measured on output rather than outcomes. You'll share accountability with Sales for win rate, deal size, and expansion revenue.

    Industry observers note that needing extensive approval before acting. You'll be trusted to make calls on speed versus quality and to explain your reasoning.

    Discomfort with direct, candid feedback, especially from sellers on what's working in live deals.

    We're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time—so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    Recent findings suggest that kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we’re hiring at our level 4 ($166,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    In a recent development, we cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance aims through Aetna.

    $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Manufacturer-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    Winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

    Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    It has been revealed that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Recent findings suggest that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Stations in Newly introduced Hampshire, Wisconsin, Massachusetts, and Utah all climbed in our regular ranking of public radio stations between July and September.

    It has been revealed that more than a year ago, NHPR reporter Todd Bookman started asking questions about “an irregular personnel maneuver” involving the chief justice of Latest Hampshire’s Supreme Court. Bookman’s reporting ultimately became “Exhibit A” in the ethics probe that led to the justice’s resignation in September.

    The bombshell resignation news was NHPR’s biggest story in September — and of 2026 to date. The story helped push NHPR up several spots in our regular ranking of public radio websites. NHPR saw visits rise 22% that month, according to Similarweb visit figures compiled by Nieman Lab.

    RELATED ARTICLECollaborations and primary elections boosted traffic to public media sites this quarterNeel DhaneshaJuly 29, 2026At the very top of the list, not much moved. The Chicago Sun-Times, owned by Chicago Public Media, held onto the top spot, followed by Gothamist (from WNYC) and Minnesota Public Radio. As Nieman Lab senior writer Joshua Benton wrote when introducing the rankings, which we’ve also done for local newspapers and local nonprofit news sites, not all markets are created equal. Public radio stations serving major metropolitan areas with lots of college graduates have a bigger potential audience than stations serving smaller communities and areas with fewer resources. And, of course, Similarweb provides an estimate; internal metrics may differ. Still, the rankings are a valuable window into some industry-wide trends, and often an opportunity to highlight local news organizations punching above their weight.

    Like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. Newly introduced Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, said NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott. She described September as a solid month, not an outlier. “But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said. “[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added. On the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.” BREAKING: Fearless reporting by New Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp — Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026 WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September. Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, said organic search traffic and Google Discover helped. “We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell said, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.” “Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also notable to take advantage when it delivers,” she added. Those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell said. Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.” The Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15. According to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary. “We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she said. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.” And then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.” “I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.” If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers. “The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.” Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah. Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total users are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill. All in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill said. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case. “Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill said. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%. Two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit. “We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.” Sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story.     📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (449 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Google Notes Back Button Hijacking Policy Covers Social Visits via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (449 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google’s back button hijacking policy applies whenever the hijacking happens in a browser, including on visits from social media rather than Google Search, according to an FAQ Google added to its spam policies today.
    • Ad platform code is still allowed, the FAQ says, and Google acts only on pages that show the hijacking.
    • Google’s Search Central changelog claims the FAQ answers common questions it has received about the policy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google’s back button hijacking policy applies whenever the hijacking happens in a browser, including on visits from social media rather than Google Search, according to an FAQ Google added to its spam policies today.

    Ad platform code is still allowed, the FAQ says, and Google acts only on pages that show the hijacking.

    Google’s Search Central changelog claims the FAQ answers common questions it has received about the policy. I covered the policy when Google unveiled it in April, with enforcement set to start June 15.

    Industry observers note that one FAQ question asks whether the back button hijacking policy covers people who arrive from a non-Search channel, such as social media, and then can’t get back to where they came from. Google wrote:.

    “If back button hijacking happens when a user is browsing within a browser, then the policy applies.”.

    A separate answer states “Discover is a part of Google Search and our spam policies apply to Discover as well.” That answer covers Google’s spam policies in general, not only this one.

    For a website that opens an external app, which then keeps the user from getting back to the site, the FAQ states “app navigation and ‘open in app’ behaviors are outside the scope of the back button hijacking policy.”.

    Google’s FAQ reveals how the policy applies to visits in a browser and where external app navigation falls outside its scope.

    Google’s April announcement said some back button hijacking “may originate from the site’s included libraries or advertising platform,” and asked sites to remove or turn off the code behind it.

    It has been revealed that the FAQ asks whether Google is preventing sites from importing code hosted by advertising platforms. Google wrote:.

    “No, site owners can continue to work with advertising platforms and import code that they host. We only take action on pages that exhibit back button hijacking behavior.”.

    A back button test that starts from a Google results page doesn’t cover every visit the hijacking policy applies to. Test pages that carry ad code by arriving from a social media link and pressing back, and repeat it from Discover when one of your pages indicates up there.

    Google’s answer on ad code lets you keep your ad partners. The thing to remove is the code or setting on a page that interferes with the back button, wherever it comes from.

    In a recent development, google’s FAQ also says owners can report back button hijacking through its spam report form. Those reports go toward improving Google’s spam detection systems, which gives people who hit hijacking on a social or Discover visit a way to flag a site.

    From YouTube views to crypto hacks, subscription cyclones to Czech hats: Have you kept up with this week’s media news?

    It’s been yet another busy week. Recap it with the fourth edition of the Nieman Lab News-About-News Quiz, your weekly incentive to keep up with the latest happenings in the world of digital journalism. All questions are based on the week’s Nieman Lab stories or articles elsewhere that we’ve linked to in What We’re Reading. This is the final edition of the quiz for 2026; if people seem to like it, we’ll keep it going in 2027. Good luck!

    The Chicago Sun-Times declared a fresh slogan this week. What is it?

    “Chicago’s Paper” replaces “The Hardest-Working Paper in America,” the paper’s slogan since 2018.

    An “overwhelming majority” of American journalists employed by this tech giant voted this week to authorize a strike.

    “The union has been negotiating a fresh contract for more than a year, and leaders say disagreements over wages, artificial intelligence and manager overreach have forced them to take this step.”.

    A “digital experience platform” organization whose software runs on many news sites was hacked this week, sending malware to readers of the BBC, CNN, and Fox News. What’s the company’s name?

    The hack stole cryptocurrency and credit card numbers from an unknown number of news site visitors.

    According to recent reports, A major journalism school announced this week that its master’s degree programs would now be tuition-free for in-state residents. Which school?

    “Newmark J-School’s campaign for free tuition is rooted in CUNY’s decades-long commitment to access and opportunity for New Yorkers. At a time of profound transformation in the news industry, removing the cost of tuition makes it easier for more people to take the risk of entering the field.”.

    According to recent reports, at this week’s summit in China, Bloomberg TV reporter Annmarie Hordern asked Donald Trump whether he felt Nvidia founder Jensen Huang had been disloyal to the United States. What happened next?

    “It was the latest example of China’s strict controls on news coverage and how tightly Beijing tries to stage-manage major international events.”.

    Paid digital subscriptions at McClatchy-owned publications — a group that includes the Miami Herald, the Kansas City Star, and the Charlotte Observer — have declined how much in the past year, according to an internal corporate presentation?

    Industry observers note that unique visitors have also dropped by 39%. McClatchy’s response? Doubling down on AI.

    This is the per capita annual funding for public media across a set of five rich countries: $110, $81, $53, $27, $3. Name the five countries, in order.

    With prospects for public media brighter with a Democratic Congress, some advocates are calling for a major increase in the United States’ historically puny funding levels.

    Recent findings suggest that youTube has found a new way to inflate the number of “views” a video on its platform gets. What is it?

    “YouTube, which has become even more popular on TVs than phones, also says the change will help it align with ‘TV industry standards,’ which similarly record views by estimating the number of people watching demonstrates.”.

    In Czechia, mass rallies in support of public broadcasting have featured protestors wearing a very specific hat. Whose hat is it?

    Sources indicate that since 1965, Večerníček (a diminutive of večerník, meaning evening newspaper) has appeared on Czech Television every night at 6:45 p.m. to wish children goodnight. Demonstrators wore his hat during the country’s largest protests since 1989 to oppose government intends to scrap public media license fees.
